QUESTION PRESENTED 

Under this Court’s decision in Yearsley v. W.A. Ross 
Construction  Co.,  contractors  have  a  defense  to  liability 
for damages caused by “lawfully” carrying out work that 
is “authorized and directed” by the government. 309 U.S. 
18, 20, 22 (1940).  

The  question  presented  is:  Are  interlocutory  orders 
holding that a contractor does not meet the requirements 
for  a  defense  under  Yearsley  immediately  appealable 
under the collateral order doctrine?

- 1 - 

INTRODUCTION 

GEO asks this Court to review an unpublished decision 
holding what every published opinion to have considered 
the question has held: There is no exception to the final-
judgment rule for private contractors asserting a defense 
under Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co., 309 U.S. 
18 (1940). This Court should decline GEO’s request.  

Yearsley shields government contractors from liability 
for  actions  that  were  authorized  and  directed  by  the 
government.  Determining  whether  the  defense  applies 
typically  requires  a  fact-intensive  inquiry  into  what  the 
contractor did and whether the government directed it to 
do  so.  Take  this  case:  To  determine  whether  summary 
judgment was warranted on GEO’s Yearsley defense, the 
district court reviewed hundreds of pages of documents, 
numerous  deposition  transcripts  and  declarations,  and 
dozens of discovery responses.  

In an unpublished order, the Tenth Circuit dismissed 
GEO’s  appeal  of  the  district  court’s  summary  judgment 
decision for lack of appellate jurisdiction. This conclusion 
is a straightforward application of the final-judgment rule. 
Courts of appeals may only review “final decisions of the 
district  courts.”  28  U.S.C.  §  1291  (emphasis  added). 
Denials of summary judgment ordinarily don’t count.  

The  collateral  order  doctrine  provides  a  “narrow 
exception”  to  this  rule.  Digit.  Equip.  Corp.  v.  Desktop 
Direct, 511 U.S. 863, 868 (1994). But that narrow exception 
applies  only  to  orders  that  meet  three  stringent 
requirements: They must be conclusive; they must resolve 
important questions completely separate from the merits; 
and they must render such important questions effectively 
unreviewable  on  appeal  from  final  judgment  in  the 
underlying action.

- 2 - 

Yearsley orders, the Tenth Circuit held, fail the second 
requirement.  As  this  case  demonstrates,  reviewing  a 
district  court’s  Yearsley  order  will  almost  inevitably 
require a fact-intensive inquiry that cannot be completely 
separated from the merits. After all, it is hard to imagine 
a  case  where  what  the  contractor  did  and  whether  the 
government told it do so have no bearing on the merits of 
the claims. Yearsley orders, therefore, do not fall within 
the  narrow  category  of  interlocutory  decisions  that  may 
be collaterally appealed.  

GEO  cannot  identify  a  single  circuit  that  has  a 
different rule. So instead it lumps together cases about the 
Yearsley  defense  with  cases  about  other  defenses  under 
the  general  label  “derivative  sovereign  immunity.”  But 
there is no conflict between the lower court’s decision that 
Yearsley  orders  are  not  collaterally  appealable  and 
decisions holding that different defenses are.

The same rule that applies to GEO applies in the slip-

warrant automatic interlocutory appeal.  

If  GEO  truly  believed  that  some  important  federal 
interest justified interlocutory appeal in this case, it could 
have  asked  for  permission  to  file  one  under  28  U.S.C. 
§ 1292  or  it  could  have  sought  mandamus.  This  Court

STATEMENT 

A.  Legal Background 

1.  The Yearsley defense 

This  Court  has  long  held  that  the  United  States’ 
sovereign “immunity does not extend to those that act[] in 
its  name.”  Sloan  Shipyards  Corp.  v.  U.S.  Shipping  Bd. 
Emergency Fleet Corp., 258 U.S. 549, 567-68 (1922); see, 
e.g.,  Keifer  &  Keifer  v.  Reconstruction  Fin.  Corp., 
306 U.S.  381,  388  (1939)  (“[T]he  government  does  not 
become  the  conduit  of  its  immunity  in  suits  against  its 
agents  or  instrumentalities  merely  because  they  do  its 
work.”); Campbell-Ewald Co. v. Gomez, 577 U.S. 153, 166 
(2016). An agent of the government “does not cease to be 
answerable for his acts,” simply because he works for the 
government. Sloan Shipyards, 258 U.S. at 566-67.1 

This  accords  with  basic  agency  law:  Like  any  other 
principal, the government may delegate to its agents its 
“privilege”  to  take  actions  that  would  be  unlawful  if 
committed  by  others.  See,  e.g.,  Restatement  (Second)  of 
Agency  §  217  cmt.  a  (Am.  L.  Inst.  1958).  Here,  for 
example,  the  government  has  authorized  GEO  to  detain 
people  awaiting  immigration  proceedings.  Cf.  id.  But  a 
principal cannot delegate its immunity. See id. § 217 cmt. 
b. The government is no different. See Campbell-Ewald, 
577 U.S. at 166 (explaining that there is “no authority for 
the  notion  that  private  persons  performing  Government 
work acquire the Government’s embracive immunity”). 

While this Court has therefore repeatedly rejected the 
claim that contractors share the government’s sovereign

other  principal-agent  relationships,  a  contractor  that  is 
sued  for  damages  caused  by  simply  executing  a  lawful

by arguing that the government (the principal) and not the 
contractor (the agent) is responsible. See Yearsley v. W.A. 
Ross Constr. Co., 309 U.S. 18, 21 (1940). 

This  Court  first  recognized  this  defense  almost  a 
century  ago  in  Yearsley.  Id.  In  that  case,  a  construction

directed.  Yearsley,  309  U.S.  at  20;  United  States  Br., 
Yearsley, 1939 WL 48388, at *6 (“[I]t was intended to be 
washed away as a necessary part of the federal project for 
the stabilization of the river.”).

This Court held that, under those circumstances, the 
contractor  had  “no  liability”  for  simply  “executing  [the 
government’s] will.” Yearsley, 309 U.S. at 21. Yearsley did 
not afford the contractor sovereign immunity, derivative 
or  otherwise.  See  id.  In  fact,  the  Court  held  that  the 
government’s  authorization  to  the  contractor  to  wash

- 6 - 

away  the  plaintiffs’  land  was  only  valid  because  the 
government  itself  would  pay  the  damages—that  is, 
because the government was not immune. Id. at 22. There 
was thus no sovereign immunity to derive. 

The Court did hold, however, that the contractor had a 
defense  to  “liability.”  Id.  at  20-21  (emphasis  added). 
Government  contractors  are  not  liable  for  damages  if: 
(1) the  government  “validly”  authorized  the  contractor’s 
work;  and  (2)  the  government  “directed”  the  challenged 
conduct. Id.; accord Campbell-Ewald, 577 U.S. at 153; see 
also  Corr.  Servs.  Corp.  v.  Malesko,  534  U.S.  61,  74  n.6 
(2001) (“Where the government has directed a contractor 
to  do  the  very  thing  that  is  the  subject  of  the  claim,  we 
have recognized this as a special circumstance where the 
contractor may assert a defense.”). 

While  Yearsley  was  the  first  case  from  this  Court  to 
recognize  this  defense  in  the  government-contractor 
context,  courts  have  long  provided  agents  a  defense  to 
liability  when  it  is,  in  fact,  the  principal  that  is  truly  at 
fault—that is, when the principal directed the challenged 
conduct. See, e.g., Hatch v. Trail King Indus., 656 F.3d 59, 
68 (1st Cir. 2011) (collecting cases); Bell & Son v. Kidd & 
Roberts, 63 S.E. 607, 608 (Ga. Ct. App. 1909); Daegling v. 
Gilmore,  49  Ill.  248,  249  (1868);  Restatement  (Second) 
Torts § 404 cmts. a-b (Am. L. Inst. 1965) (contractor who 
follows another’s specifications is not liable unless defect 
in specifications is obvious). 

As  with  other  principal-agent  cases,  therefore,  the 
Yearsley  defense  typically  turns  on  the  answer  to  two 
factual questions: (1) What did the contractor do to cause 
the plaintiff’s injury?; and (2) Did the government dictate 
that conduct? See, e.g., Campbell-Ewald, 577 U.S. at 168.

- 7 - 

In  the  decades  since  Yearsley,  the  defense  has  been 
most  commonly  invoked  in  run-of-the  mill  cases,  where 
the  defendant  happens  to  be  a  government  contractor. 
See,  e.g.,  Campbell-Ewald,  577  U.S.  at  166  (Telephone 
Consumer  Protection  Act  case  against  contractor  for 
sending unwanted text messages); Evans v. Mayer Tree 
Serv., Inc., 162 N.E.3d 70 (Mass. App. Ct. 2020) (trespass 
action  against  tree-removal  company);  Johnson-Howard 
v. AECOM Spec. Missions Servs., Inc., 2023 WL 6216604 
(D. Md. Sept. 25, 2023) (slip-and-fall case against janitorial 
company);  Budrow  v.  Ames,  1998  WL  328423  (Conn. 
Super.  June  10,  1998)  (personal  injury  case  against 
architect). 

2.  The collateral order doctrine 

The question presented here is not about the Yearsley 
defense  itself.  The  question  is  whether,  when  a  district 
court  concludes  that  a  contractor  has  not  satisfied 
Yearsley’s  requirements,  that  contractor  may  take  an 
interlocutory  appeal.  And  that  question  turns  on  the 
collateral order doctrine. 

a.  The  collateral  order  doctrine  allows  immediate 
appeal  of  a  “narrow  class  of  decisions  that  do  not 
terminate the litigation, but are sufficiently important and 
collateral  to  the  merits  that  they  should  nonetheless  be 
treated as final.” Will v. Hallock, 546 U.S. 345, 345 (2006).

This Court has warned that these requirements “are 
stringent” and must be “kept so.” Will, 546 U.S. at 349-50. 
Otherwise, what is meant to be a “narrow exception” will 
undermine  the  important  interests  served  by  the  final

from “saddling” their opponents with the “cost and delay”

Whether  an  order  falls  within  the  collateral-order 
doctrine is a determination made on a categorical basis, id. 
at 868, not after an “individualized jurisdictional inquiry” 
specific to the facts of a case, Coopers, 437 U.S. at 473. So, 
for an interlocutory order to be immediately appealable, 
“the  entire  category  to  which  a  claim  belongs,  without 
regard to the chance that the litigation at hand might be 
speeded,  or  a  particular  injustic[e]  averted.”  Digit. 
Equip., 511 U.S. at 868 (emphasis added). 

B.  Factual background 

GEO  is  a  publicly  traded,  for-profit  company  that 
makes  billions  of  dollars  a  year  operating  private 
detention  facilities.  One  of  these  facilities  is  the  Aurora 
Immigration  Processing  Center,  which  houses  people 
awaiting resolution of their immigration proceedings. Pet. 
App. 4a.

C.  Procedural history 

This  lawsuit  was  filed  over  a  decade  ago.  Alejandro 
Menocal,  who  had  been  detained  in  GEO’s  facility,  sued 
GEO for violating the Trafficking Victims Protection Act’s 
prohibition on forced labor and Colorado’s prohibition on 
unjust  enrichment.  Pet.  App.  6a.  GEO  has  repeatedly 
sought to delay the case. It has sought multiple stays and 
multiple interlocutory appeals. See Supp. App. Vol. 1 at 1-
39. For example, GEO appealed the district court’s class-

affirmed, and this Court denied certiorari. See Menocal v. 
GEO Grp., Inc., 882 F.3d 905, 910 (10th Cir. 2018). That 
ultimately meritless appeal took over a year.

In so holding, the court relied on the second prong of 
the  collateral-order  test:  that  an  order  must  “resolve  an

Court  concluded,  do  not.  The  court  explained  that  the

“enmeshed in the merits,” not separate. Pet. App. 19a, 21a.

INTRODUCTION 

GEO asks this Court to review an unpublished decision 
holding what every published opinion to have considered 
the question has held: There is no exception to the final-
judgment rule for private contractors asserting a defense 
under Yearsley v. W.A. Ross Construction Co., 309 U.S. 
18 (1940). This Court should decline GEO’s request.  

Yearsley shields government contractors from liability 
for  actions  that  were  authorized  and  directed  by  the 
government.  Determining  whether  the  defense  applies 
typically  requires  a  fact-intensive  inquiry  into  what  the 
contractor did and whether the government directed it to 
do  so.  Take  this  case:  To  determine  whether  summary 
judgment was warranted on GEO’s Yearsley defense, the 
district court reviewed hundreds of pages of documents, 
numerous  deposition  transcripts  and  declarations,  and 
dozens of discovery responses.  

In an unpublished order, the Tenth Circuit dismissed 
GEO’s  appeal  of  the  district  court’s  summary  judgment 
decision for lack of appellate jurisdiction. This conclusion 
is a straightforward application of the final-judgment rule. 
Courts of appeals may only review “final decisions of the 
district  courts.”  28  U.S.C.  §  1291  (emphasis  added). 
Denials of summary judgment ordinarily don’t count.  

The  collateral  order  doctrine  provides  a  “narrow 
exception”  to  this  rule.  Digit.  Equip.  Corp.  v.  Desktop 
Direct, 511 U.S. 863, 868 (1994). But that narrow exception 
applies  only  to  orders  that  meet  three  stringent 
requirements: They must be conclusive; they must resolve 
important questions completely separate from the merits; 
and they must render such important questions effectively 
unreviewable  on  appeal  from  final  judgment  in  the 
underlying action.  

 
 - 2 - 

Yearsley orders, the Tenth Circuit held, fail the second 
requirement.  As  this  case  demonstrates,  reviewing  a 
district  court’s  Yearsley  order  will  almost  inevitably 
require a fact-intensive inquiry that cannot be completely 
separated from the merits. After all, it is hard to imagine 
a  case  where  what  the  contractor  did  and  whether  the 
government told it do so have no bearing on the merits of 
the claims. Yearsley orders, therefore, do not fall within 
the  narrow  category  of  interlocutory  decisions  that  may 
be collaterally appealed.

there is no conflict between the lower court’s decision that 
Yearsley  orders  are  not  collaterally  appealable  and 
decisions holding that different defenses are.

Yearsley has been on the books for eighty-five years. 
Yet,  in  nearly  a  century,  only  two  circuits  have  issued 
published  decisions  on  whether  an  order  rejecting  a 
contractor’s Yearsley defense is immediately appealable. 
And  they  agree  on  the  answer:  No.  See  Childs  v.  San 
Diego  Fam.  Hous.  LLC,  22  F.4th  1092,  1098  (9th  Cir.

775 F. App’x 758, 759 (4th Cir. 2019) (unpublished decision

came to the same conclusion. Pet. App. 3a.5

judgment.” Id.  at  349.  These  “conditions  are  stringent.” 
Id. And the Yearsley defense does not satisfy any of them.  

1. As the Tenth Circuit correctly held, the inquiry can 
begin and end with the separateness requirement. To be 
immediately  appealable,  an  order  must  be  “completely 
separate from the merits.” Van Cauwenberghe v. Biard, 
486  U.S.  517,  527  (1988)  (emphasis  added).  This 
requirement  is  strictly  construed.  Thus,  this  Court  has 
held that the denial of a forum non conveniens motion is 
too  enmeshed  with  the  merits  because  to  evaluate  “the 
relative  ease  of  access  to  sources  of  proof,  and  the 
availability of witnesses,” the court must “evaluate what 
proof  [will  be]  required.”  Id.  at  527-28.  It  has  held  that 
discovery-sanctions  orders  are  not  sufficiently  collateral 
to the merits because determining the appropriateness of 
sanctions may “require the reviewing court to inquire into 
the importance of the information sought or the adequacy 
or truthfulness of a response.” Cunningham v. Hamilton 
Cnty., 527 U.S. 198, 205 (1999). 

Reviewing  a  court’s  denial  of  a  contractor’s  Yearsley 
defense  will  ordinarily  be  far  more  enmeshed  with  the 
merits  than  determining  whether  a  lawsuit  has  been 
brought  in  an  inconvenient  forum  or  a  party  committed 
sanctionable  discovery  misconduct.  Yearsley  requires  a 
comparison  of  the  contractor’s  conduct  with  the  actions 
the  government  directed  the  contractor  to  take.  As  the 
Tenth  Circuit  explained,  those  issues  will  almost  always 
be core to the merits: A plaintiff cannot prove their claim 
without proving what the contractor actually did. And in 
most  cases,  the  contractor’s  defense  on  the  merits—its
